title: CleanClaimRx Specialty Companion Guide: OB/Gyn
audience: OB/Gyn practice owners, managers and billing staff who have already read the vendor's 'Universal Specialty Billing Framework'. No author, credential or date is given.
summary: A specialty add-on to the vendor's generic billing framework. Its thesis: an OB/Gyn practice runs three separate revenue cycles (maternity global package, gynecology office visits, gynecologic surgery) and loses money by pushing all three through one workflow. It follows a fixed eight-part template: reframe, payer mix, code risk tables, prior authorization, four documentation failures, four denial patterns, five revenue opportunities, then five operating standards and a five-step action list built on 90-day look-back audits. The operating ideas are reasonable (written payer-specific rules, visit counters, operative-note prompts, pre-bill edit checks, cost-sharing scripts at scheduling). The technical content is not reliable: it misuses the antepartum-only codes in its headline recommendation, mislabels several CPT and HCPCS codes, misstates Medicare eligibility and preventive coverage, and gives uncited revenue figures. No working templates are included. Almost nothing applies directly to a facility-based geriatrics practice.

outline.section: Section 1: The Reframe - OB/Gyn Is Not One Specialty. It Is Three Billing Environments in One Practice
outline.gist: Maternity global billing, gynecology office visits and gynecologic surgery follow different rules; running all three through one workflow and one skill set leaks revenue.

outline.section: Section 2: The Payer Mix Reality in OB/Gyn
outline.gist: Medicaid maternity pays below cost, commercial global-package handling varies by contract, Medicare gynecology needs separate rules; includes a six-row payer challenge table.

outline.section: Section 3: The Procedure Code Risk Profile in OB/Gyn
outline.gist: Tables of what the global obstetric package includes, 14 obstetric and 13 surgical CPT codes with billing notes, plus preventive-versus-problem visit coding.

outline.section: Section 4: Prior Authorization in OB/Gyn - Three Different Authorization Landscapes
outline.gist: Maternity intake verification and delivery notice, the documentation file for hysterectomy authorization, and diagnosis mismatches on LEEP authorizations.

outline.section: Section 5: The Documentation Failures Unique to OB/Gyn
outline.gist: Untracked antepartum visit counts, operative notes lacking code-determining detail, extra postpartum visits never billed, LEEP records missing the pathology chain.

outline.section: Section 6: The Denial Patterns Unique to OB/Gyn
outline.gist: Split global packages, preventive-versus-diagnostic errors, surgical bundling denials and procedures that differ from the authorization, each with a prevention routine.

outline.section: Section 7: The Revenue Opportunities Most OB/Gyn Practices Are Missing
outline.gist: Extra antepartum visits, postpartum depression management, ultrasound technical component, contraceptive device plus insertion billing, and office hysteroscopy, with uncited dollar estimates.

outline.section: Section 8: What Revenue Cycle Excellence Looks Like in OB/Gyn
outline.gist: Five operating standards and a five-step starter list built on visit counting, 90-day claim look-backs, an operative-note review and a scheduling script.

framework_elements: Separate workflow per billing environment (service line)
Payer-by-payer reference document for bundled packages
Coverage and benefit verification at first visit
Payer notification of a delivery or admission event
Referral and co-management authorization ownership
Surgical prior-authorization file assembly
Authorization-to-claim diagnosis and procedure matching
Intraoperative change notification to authorization staff
Retroactive authorization requests
Visit counter with threshold flag for bundled packages
Capture of services outside a global package
Transfer-of-care (split package) billing protocol
Structured operative note template with code-determining prompts
Preventive-plus-problem visit coding with modifier 25
Medicare preventive and screening code selection
ABN use for frequency-limited Medicare services (named only)
Pre-bill NCCI edit check on multi-procedure claims
Device-plus-procedure charge pairing audit
Cost-sharing counseling at scheduling
Self-pay package deposit and scope counseling
Problem-visit capture during a global period
Screening-to-management documentation (depression)
Professional versus technical component billing for in-office imaging
Imaging accreditation
Site-of-service choice for procedures (office versus operating room)
Quarterly charge-capture and coding audits
90-day retrospective claim review with corrected claims
Joint billing-clinician documentation review
Patient billing complaint tracking
Payer-mix margin awareness (below-cost Medicaid lines)

processes.name: Antepartum visit counting and overage flag
steps: Flag high-risk pregnancies at intake
Count every antepartum visit in an EHR field or tracking sheet
Raise a billing review when the count passes 13
Bill the extra visits (document says 59425/59426; standard guidance is problem E/M codes for complications)
Audit counts and separately billable capture quarterly
processes.owner_role: Billing staff with clinical intake (document names no owner)

processes.name: Global package verification at maternity intake
steps: Verify plan coverage of the global package, rate, visits included and postpartum window at the first prenatal visit
Counsel the patient on expected financial responsibility
Flag likely split-package cases early
Put delivery notification into the hospital workflow
Settle who holds any maternal-fetal medicine referral authorization
Obtain authorization for scheduled cerclage or version where required
processes.owner_role: Front desk or intake staff with billing
processes.cadence: Per new obstetric patient; notification within 24-48 hours of delivery

processes.name: Split-package (transfer of care) handling
steps: Write a transfer protocol recording visits, who bills which component and the handoff date
On transfer out, bill the antepartum-only component promptly
On transfer in, obtain records with the visit count and confirm the split before billing delivery
Flag every delivery where the delivering physician did not give all antepartum care

processes.name: Hysterectomy authorization file
steps: Document failed conservative treatment from the first presentation
Attach imaging with size and location of pathology
Match the diagnosis code exactly to the pathology
Confirm surgeon and approach meet the payer's rules
Submit the complete file before scheduling

processes.name: Intraoperative finding notification
steps: Surgeon reports any procedure added or changed from what was authorized
Authorization team notifies the payer in real time or within 24 hours
Request retroactive authorization
Keep a record of the notification

processes.name: Pre-bill surgical code review against NCCI edits
steps: List the planned code combination for the encounter
Check each code pair against NCCI edits
Add a modifier only where a distinct site or procedure is documented
Maintain a list of the practice's recurring pairs that need review
Submit the claim
processes.cadence: Every multi-procedure surgical claim; 90-day look-back at start

processes.name: Preventive-plus-problem visit handling
steps: Warn the patient at scheduling that a separate concern may create an added charge
Clinician documents the problem work separately from the preventive service
Bill the preventive code plus a problem E/M with modifier 25
Use Medicare-specific preventive and screening codes for Medicare patients
Track unexpected-charge complaints for 90 days and revise the script

processes.name: Quarterly LARC billing audit
steps: Pull every IUD and implant insertion for the period
Confirm both the device code and the insertion code were billed
Confirm both were paid
Rebill any missing component
Report dollars recovered
processes.cadence: Quarterly; first pass covers the last 90 days

metrics.name: Antepartum visit count per pregnancy
metrics.definition: Running count of prenatal visits compared with the number the global package includes
metrics.formula: count of antepartum visits per patient
metrics.target: 13 included; billing review triggered at visit 14
metrics.red_flag: High-risk patient past 13 visits with no separate claim

metrics.name: Unbilled antepartum overage revenue
metrics.definition: Estimated yearly revenue from visits beyond the global count
metrics.formula: deliveries x share high-risk x average extra visits x payment per visit (150 x 30% x 4 x $80-$120)

metrics.name: LARC device-and-procedure capture
metrics.definition: Whether each IUD or implant insertion has both the device code and the insertion code billed and paid

metrics.name: LARC audit recovery
metrics.definition: Dollars recovered by the quarterly LARC audit

metrics.name: Unexpected-charge complaint rate
metrics.definition: Patient complaints about surprise charges after preventive-plus-problem visits
metrics.target: Significant drop within 90 days of introducing the scheduling script
metrics.red_flag: No drop, meaning the script needs rewriting

metrics.name: Delivery notification timeliness
metrics.definition: Time from delivery to payer notification
metrics.red_flag: Missed window delays claim processing and lengthens receivables

metrics.name: Intraoperative deviation notification time
metrics.definition: Time from an unplanned or changed procedure to notifying the authorization team
metrics.target: Real time, no later than 24 hours

metrics.name: NCCI pre-bill check coverage
metrics.definition: Share of multi-procedure surgical encounters checked against NCCI edits before submission
metrics.red_flag: Code pairs denied for a missing modifier

metrics.name: Operative-note documentation gaps
metrics.definition: Note gaps that caused coder queries or code downgrades in the last six months
metrics.target: Top three gaps get dictation-template prompts

metrics.name: Ultrasound technical-component revenue
metrics.definition: Added yearly revenue from billing ultrasound globally instead of professional component only
metrics.formula: scans per week x 52 x technical-component payment
metrics.target: $60,000-$100,000 or more a year at 20 scans per week

metrics.name: Audit cadence for obstetric charge capture
metrics.definition: How often antepartum counts, separately billable procedures and postpartum billing are audited

numeric_claims.claim: Medicaid covers 40 to 50 percent of births in many U.S. markets and more than 60 percent in some.
Medicaid global obstetric payment is below the cost of care in most states.
Medicare patients are by definition over 65, and Medicare does not cover obstetric services.
Payers want delivery notification within 24 to 48 hours ('some' payers in Section 2, 'most' in Section 4).
The global package includes up to 13 antepartum visits for both vaginal and cesarean delivery.
The global package includes one postpartum office visit within six weeks.
59425 covers 4-6 and 59426 covers 7 or more 'additional' antepartum visits beyond the global count.
High-risk patients may have 18, 20 or more antepartum visits.
Vaginal hysterectomy code choice turns on a uterine weight of 250 grams.
58572 is laparoscopic hysterectomy for a uterus of 250 g or less with removal of tubes and ovaries.
Most payers require prior authorization for cerclage and for external cephalic version.
Hysterectomy authorization needs at least one failed alternative treatment on record.
Many payers credential surgeons separately for open, laparoscopic and robotic hysterectomy.
150 deliveries, 30 percent high-risk, 4 extra visits each gives 180 visits; at $80-$120 that is $14,400-$21,600 a year.
Postpartum depression screening is recommended by ACOG and required by most quality programs.
A standard obstetric ultrasound (76805) pays about $120 in total under Medicare, split about equally between professional and technical components.
A practice doing 20 ultrasounds a week gains $60,000 to $100,000 or more a year by billing the technical component.
Most commercial payers require AIUM or equivalent accreditation to bill the ultrasound technical component.
Ultrasound accreditation takes three to six months and pays back within the first year.
LARC billing uses device codes J7296, J7297, J7298, J7300, J7301 or J7307 with procedure codes 58300, 58301, 11981, 11982 or 11983.
A physician can complete four office hysteroscopies in a morning versus two operating-room cases.
A quarterly LARC audit routinely recovers $500 to $2,000 per quarter.
An NCCI edit check takes five minutes per surgical claim.
Unplanned intraoperative procedures should be reported to the authorization team within 24 hours.
Readers who see their gaps are ahead of where most peers will be in five years.

checkable_claims.claim: Visits beyond that count ... are separately billable using CPT 59425 (4-6 additional antepartum visits) or 59426 (7 or more additional antepartum visits).
checkable_claims.section: Section 5, Documentation Failure 1 (repeated in Sections 3, 7 and 8)
checkable_claims.why: This is the document's top revenue recommendation. CPT and ACOG guidance treat 59425/59426 as antepartum-only codes for a provider who does not deliver; billing them alongside a global code is unbundling and creates repayment exposure.

checkable_claims.claim: 58572: Laparoscopic hysterectomy, uterus 250g or less, with BSO - BSO included; do not bill 58661 separately.
checkable_claims.section: Section 3, gynecologic surgical code table (repeated in Section 6)
checkable_claims.why: CPT defines 58572 as uterus over 250 g without adnexal removal. Coding from this table selects a code the service does not support.

checkable_claims.claim: Medicare ... covers ... annual well-woman exams under the Medicare preventive benefit ... gynecologic preventive services (pap smear G0101, pelvic exam Q0091).
checkable_claims.why: The two descriptors appear reversed, and Medicare screening pelvic and Pap coverage is every 24 months for most women rather than annual. Errors cause denials and missed ABNs; relevant to any Medicare primary-care practice.

checkable_claims.claim: Medicare does not cover obstetric services for its beneficiaries (Medicare patients are, by definition, over 65 and not pregnant).
checkable_claims.section: Section 2, Medicare in the GYN Practice
checkable_claims.why: Medicare enrolls disabled and ESRD beneficiaries under 65 and pays for pregnancy care. A false eligibility premise shows the Medicare content cannot be taken on trust.

checkable_claims.claim: Included in Global OB Package: Postpartum office visit (one, within 6 weeks) ... Routine newborn care (professional, if same physician).
checkable_claims.why: Newborn care is billed for the infant as a separate patient, and CPT bundles all routine postpartum care rather than a single visit. Wrong package boundaries cause both lost revenue and improper separate billing.

checkable_claims.claim: A standard obstetric ultrasound (76805) has a total Medicare payment of approximately $120 - split roughly equally between professional and technical components ... billing the technical component ... requires AIUM ... accreditation or equivalent, which most commercial payers require.
checkable_claims.why: Drives an equipment and accreditation decision and a $60,000-$100,000 projection. Medicare's accreditation mandate covers advanced imaging rather than ultrasound, and the component split is not equal.

checkable_claims.claim: N80.0 (endometriosis of uterus) and N80.1 (endometriosis of ovary) are different authorization submissions even in the same patient.
checkable_claims.why: Both became non-billable category headers when the endometriosis codes were expanded (confirmed against the FY2027 code set). A claim or authorization at this level rejects, and it dates the source material.

checkable_claims.claim: The correct billing: 99395-99397 (preventive, age-appropriate) with modifier 25 on the additional E&M code (99212-99215) for the separately identified problem.
checkable_claims.section: Section 3, Preventive vs. Diagnostic in GYN
checkable_claims.why: The same rule governs an annual wellness visit plus a problem visit in this practice. Confirm modifier placement, the documentation standard and the omitted new-patient and adolescent code ranges.

topics: modifier 25 on preventive plus problem visits
recoupment risk from miscoded preventive visits
physician time efficiency by site of service

adopt.idea: Give each distinct billing environment its own written workflow instead of one generic process.
adopt.why: Rules, payer behavior and documentation needs differ by service line, and skill in one does not carry over to another.
adopt.note: Here the environments are hospital inpatient, skilled nursing and nursing facility, assisted living and home, and time-based care-management codes.

adopt.idea: Keep a payer-by-payer reference sheet for bundled or specially processed services and review it at every contract renewal.
adopt.why: Turns tribal knowledge about each plan's quirks into rules a new hire or an AI agent can follow.
adopt.note: Build it for UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Capital Health Plan, Florida Blue, the Medicaid plans, VA and Tricare, covering care management, wellness visits, ACP and facility visits.

adopt.idea: Attach a running counter to any service with an included quantity or frequency limit, with an automatic flag at the threshold.
adopt.why: Thresholds get missed when nobody is counting; a counter turns a rule into an alert.
adopt.note: No maternity work, but the mechanism fits wellness-visit eligibility dates, monthly care-management minutes, ACP minutes and required nursing-facility visit intervals.

adopt.idea: When a preventive visit also addresses a problem, document and bill the problem work separately with modifier 25 and tell the patient in advance about possible cost-sharing.
adopt.why: Captures legitimate work and heads off billing complaints.
adopt.note: The direct analog is an annual wellness visit plus a problem-oriented visit on the same day; verify Medicare and plan rules rather than relying on this document.

adopt.idea: Run every multi-code claim through NCCI edits before submission and keep a list of the practice's recurring code pairs.
adopt.why: Cheap prevention for predictable bundling denials.
adopt.note: Should be an automated scrubber rule in the AI billing pipeline, including Medicaid NCCI and payer-specific edits.

adopt.idea: Open each improvement with a 90-day retrospective audit that sizes the leak, rebills what is still within filing limits and justifies a permanent control.
adopt.why: Produces a dollar figure and a baseline instead of an assumption.
adopt.note: Check each payer's corrected-claim and timely-filing limits first; the document does not.

adopt.idea: Have clinicians and billing staff design note templates together so they prompt for the facts that decide code selection.
adopt.why: Notes written only for clinical continuity often cannot support the code billed.
adopt.note: Applies to facility visit notes, care-management time logs and ACP notes.

adopt.idea: Use a written handoff protocol whenever care is split between providers, recording who bills which component and from what date.
adopt.why: Prevents duplicate-claim denials when two parties bill overlapping packages.
adopt.note: Relevant to physician and nurse practitioner split visits, covering providers, attending changes at facilities and one-biller-per-month care-management codes.

adopt.idea: Notify the authorization or billing function immediately when the service delivered differs from what was authorized.
adopt.why: Retroactive approval is far more likely when a contemporaneous notice exists.
adopt.note: Few of the practice's own services need authorization; mainly relevant to Medicare Advantage facility stays and ordered services.

adopt.idea: Evaluate equipment-based ancillary services for technical-component revenue.
adopt.why: Owning the equipment can capture revenue otherwise referred out.
adopt.note: Facility-based practice with no office; the document's ultrasound numbers are also unreliable.

practice_relevance.why: The practice has no obstetric, gynecologic surgery, office procedure or imaging work and almost no point-of-service collections. Only operating patterns transfer: separate workflows per billing environment, threshold counters, modifier 25 logic for a wellness visit plus a problem visit, pre-bill edit checks and look-back audits. The Medicare passages that might have applied are wrong.
sections_that_do_not_apply: Section 2: Medicaid maternity and commercial global-package content
Section 3: obstetric and gynecologic surgical code tables
Section 4: maternity, hysterectomy and LEEP authorization
Section 5: all four documentation failures in their specifics
Section 6: split global package, surgical bundling and authorization-mismatch denials
Section 8: Standards 1, 2, 3 and 5 and Actions 1, 3 and 4

accuracy_concerns: Headline recommendation is wrong: it tells practices to bill 59425/59426 for visits past 13 on top of a global code. Those codes are for a provider who gives antepartum care only (one unit for 4-6 or 7+ visits). Extra visits for complications are billed as problem E/M visits; extra routine visits are not billable. Repeated in Sections 3, 5, 7 and 8.

58572 is described as uterus 250 g or less with BSO. CPT defines it as uterus over 250 g; 58571 is 250 g or less with tubes or ovaries and 58573 is over 250 g with tubes or ovaries. Repeated in Section 6.

G0101 and Q0091 descriptors are swapped (G0101 is the screening pelvic and breast exam; Q0091 is Pap specimen collection). Medicare has no 'annual well-woman exam'; screening pelvic/Pap is every 24 months unless high risk.

'Medicare patients are, by definition, over 65' and 'Medicare does not cover obstetric services' are both false. Medicare enrolls disabled and ESRD beneficiaries under 65 and pays for pregnancy and delivery care.
Routine newborn care is listed inside the maternity global package. Newborn care belongs to a separate patient and is billed separately.
'One postpartum visit within six weeks' understates CPT, which bundles routine postpartum hospital and office care; payer windows vary.
Cerclage 'placement or removal (59320, 59325)': both codes are placement (vaginal and abdominal). Removal has its own code.

Colposcopy coding is muddled: 57420 (vaginal colposcopy) is cited as the code bundled into LEEP, when the cervical colposcopy family starts at 57452; 57460 (loop biopsy) and 57461 (loop conization) are blurred.
N80.0 and N80.1, offered as models of diagnosis specificity, are category headers that are not valid for claims (verified against the FY2027 ICD-10-CM set).

Ultrasound: says technical-component billing needs accreditation that most commercial payers require and that Medicare payment splits equally. Medicare's accreditation mandate covers CT, MRI and nuclear imaging, not ultrasound; payer rules vary; fee schedule values put the technical component well above half. Practices that own the machine normally bill globally already.

Payer 'credentialing' of surgeons by approach (open, laparoscopic, robotic) is presented as common. Approach-specific privileges are granted by hospitals, and robotic cases use the laparoscopic CPT codes. This looks invented.

'Most payers' requiring prior authorization for cerclage and external cephalic version, and routine LEEP authorizations, are asserted with no source and do not match typical payer authorization lists.

Postpartum depression: proposes modifier 25 on a visit that is itself inside the global (no E/M is billed for it), and never names the screening code or the behavioral health integration codes it alludes to.
Office hysteroscopy: claims the gain is not in procedure reimbursement, ignoring the large office (non-facility) payment differential that is the real economic driver.
Treats Medicaid as paying a global obstetric fee everywhere; many state programs and plans require itemized or split billing.
Preventive code range given (99395-99397) covers established adult patients only; new-patient and adolescent codes are omitted.
internal_contradictions: The code table defines 59425/59426 as antepartum-only, partial-package codes, while four other passages use them for 'additional' visits on top of a global.
Antepartum overage is called the largest missed revenue item at $14,400-$21,600 a year, yet the ultrasound item is valued at $60,000-$100,000 or more.
Overage revenue is priced per visit ($80-$120 x 180 visits) although the codes it names are single-unit bundles covering a range of visits.
Section 2 says 'some' payers require delivery notice within 24-48 hours; Section 4 says 'most'.
Office hysteroscopy reimbursement is called substantially higher, then the benefit is said not to lie in procedure reimbursement.
58571 and 58572 are both described as 250 g or less with adnexal removal.
LARC is 'among the highest-reimbursement office procedures', yet the audit that catches missed components is said to recover only $500-$2,000 a quarter.
Says Medicare covers an annual well-woman exam, then says Medicare preventive rules differ and lists separate screening codes that are not annual.
time_sensitive_or_outdated: ICD-10-CM endometriosis codes N80.0 and N80.1 were expanded in October 2022 and are no longer billable at that level.
The single six-week postpartum visit model predates ACOG's 2018 postpartum guidance and the 12-month Medicaid postpartum coverage most states have adopted.
The 76805 Medicare payment and $80-$120 commercial visit rate are undated; the 2026 physician fee schedule changed conversion factors and practice-expense allocation.
No mention of prior-authorization decision deadlines that took effect in 2026 for Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care plans.
No mention of good-faith estimate duties for self-pay maternity packages under the No Surprises Act.
HCPCS device codes and payer authorization lists change quarterly; the document carries no 'as of' date.
ai_generation_signals: Identical eight-section skeleton, 'Five Non-Negotiable Operational Standards' and 'Prioritized Five-Action Implementation List' as the oncology guide, ending in an aphorism box.
Superlatives recycled across the series: each specialty is declared the most complex in outpatient medicine.
Constant 'this is not X, it is Y' constructions and sweeping absolutes about what 'most practices' do.
Tidy round-number scenarios with no source (150 deliveries, 30 percent, 4 visits; 20 scans a week).
Confident but wrong code descriptors (58572, G0101/Q0091, 59320/59325) typical of pattern completion rather than a codebook.
Cross-reference to an 'Orthopedics Companion Guide', suggesting one template filled in per specialty.
No author, credential, date, citation, payer name or state anywhere; roughly 160 words per page across 41 pages.
missing_for_real_use: None of the tools it prescribes is supplied: no visit counter, operative note template, payer reference matrix, transfer protocol or audit worksheet; the scheduling script is one sentence.
No citations to CPT guidelines, ACOG coding guidance, the NCCI policy manual, CMS manuals or any payer policy.
Modifiers other than 25 (22, 24, 51, 59 and X modifiers, assistant surgeon, TH), multiple-gestation delivery coding and surgical global periods.
State Medicaid maternity billing rules, and the sterilization consent and hysterectomy acknowledgment forms that drive Medicaid surgical denials.
Medicare screening frequency limits and how to use an ABN, although ABNs are named.
Quality-reporting codes for prenatal and postpartum visits and the depression screening code.
KPI definitions, benchmarks, staffing roles and system configuration steps.
Appeal language, denial reason codes and corrected-claim filing limits for the look-back audits it recommends.
